scenes.narration: Do you know why an AI Agent can become less useful after it remembers more? Keep it in mind.
scenes.headline: Do you know why an AI Agent gets worse with more memory?

scenes.narration: Microsoft Research calls this the raw-history problem: long interaction logs mix useful experience with details that no longer matter. Preserve the trace, but turn its decision-relevant parts into reusable knowledge.
scenes.headline: Microsoft Research: raw history can bury useful experience
scenes.coreLabel: Raw logs mix signal and noise

scenes.narration: Then the Agent searches a larger pile, spends context on noise, and can miss the fact or constraint that should change its next action.
scenes.headline: An AI Agent can miss the constraint that changes its next action

scenes.narration: This episode gives you an AI Agent retain–distill–forget table: a simple way to decide what stays available, what becomes a compact lesson, and what should stop competing for attention.
scenes.headline: Use an AI Agent retain–distill–forget table

scenes.narration: The goal is not perfect memory. It is decision-ready memory: the smallest set of facts and skills that helps an Agent act correctly now.
scenes.headline: Decision-ready memory beats a larger archive

scenes.narration: This video is packed with practical, high-value insights to help you get better at using AI. It's a longer one, so follow Tiny Agent and save it so you don't lose it.
scenes.headline: Practical, high-value AI Agent methods

scenes.narration: Chapter two: Raw History. Learn why a complete log is not automatically a useful memory.
scenes.headline: Chapter 2: Raw History
scenes.coreLabel: A complete log is not a useful prompt

scenes.narration: An interaction record can contain a decision, a failed search, copied text, an obsolete plan, and a temporary tool error all at once. Those items deserve different treatment because they answer different future questions.
scenes.headline: One record can mix decisions, searches, plans, and errors

scenes.narration: Keeping that record is valuable for audit and recovery. Sending all of it back into every new task is a different decision.
scenes.headline: Keep history for audit, not by default for every task

scenes.narration: The more irrelevant detail the Agent retrieves, the harder it becomes to identify the condition that actually changes the current answer.
scenes.headline: Noise hides the condition that matters now

scenes.narration: That is why larger memory can feel like better recall while producing slower, less reliable reasoning. Retrieval quality matters more than the visible size of the archive.
scenes.headline: Bigger retrieval can produce slower, weaker reasoning

scenes.narration: Treat history as a source to process, not a bag that must be poured into the next context window.
scenes.headline: Process history before it reaches the context window

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, keep raw history for traceability, not as the default prompt.
scenes.headline: Chapter recap. First, keep raw history for traceability.

scenes.narration: Second, separate the value of storing an event from the value of retrieving it now.
scenes.headline: Second, separate storage value from retrieval value.

scenes.narration: Third, judge memory by whether it improves the next decision.
scenes.headline: Third, judge memory by the next decision.

scenes.narration: Chapter three: Useful Units. Turn experience into things an AI Agent can reuse.
scenes.headline: Chapter 3: Useful Units

scenes.narration: The Microsoft Research article describes a shift from storing text chunks toward structured knowledge.
scenes.headline: Shift from text chunks toward structured knowledge

scenes.narration: One useful unit is a fact: a verified constraint, a current setting, or a result that narrows what the Agent can safely do. It should also name the scope in which that conclusion remains trustworthy.
scenes.headline: Facts preserve verified constraints and results

scenes.narration: Another is a reusable skill: a compact procedure that says when to take an action, what evidence to collect, and when to stop.
scenes.headline: Skills preserve repeatable action patterns

scenes.narration: Facts answer what is true enough for this task. Skills answer how to proceed when the same pattern appears again.
scenes.headline: Facts narrow choices; skills guide work

scenes.narration: This transformation removes repeated narration without throwing away the lesson contained in the interaction.
scenes.headline: Remove repetition without losing the lesson

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, promote verified facts out of raw transcripts.
scenes.headline: Chapter recap. First, extract verified facts.

scenes.narration: Second, capture repeatable procedures as skills, not anecdotes.
scenes.headline: Second, write repeatable skills.

scenes.narration: Third, keep each unit small enough to guide one future decision.
scenes.headline: Third, give each unit one decision job.

scenes.narration: Chapter four: Task Routing. Retrieve only the knowledge that belongs to the task in front of you.
scenes.headline: Chapter 4: Task Routing
scenes.coreLabel: Retrieve for the task at hand

scenes.narration: PlugMem uses high-level concepts and inferred intent as routing signals instead of returning long passages by default.
scenes.headline: Route with current goal, entity, risk, and next action

scenes.narration: In practical terms, start with the current goal, the entity, the risk, and the next action that needs support. These cues shrink retrieval before the Agent begins comparing evidence.
scenes.headline: Do not retrieve every record with a broad keyword

scenes.narration: Use those cues to select a few relevant facts and skills. Do not retrieve every record that shares a broad keyword.
scenes.headline: Select a few facts and skills that change this decision

scenes.narration: Before the selected memory reaches the base Agent, distill it into concise guidance: what is known, what matters, and what must still be checked.
scenes.headline: Distill retrieval into concise action guidance

scenes.narration: If the answer depends on live information, retrieval is not enough. The Agent still needs fresh evidence from the appropriate source.
scenes.headline: Live questions still require fresh evidence

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, route memory from the current decision, not from a vague topic match.
scenes.headline: Chapter recap. First, route from the decision.

scenes.narration: Second, pass compact guidance instead of a transcript.
scenes.headline: Second, pass guidance instead of transcripts.

scenes.narration: Third, use fresh evidence whenever the task can change over time.
scenes.headline: Third, refresh changeable facts.

scenes.narration: Chapter five: Memory Lifecycle. Decide whether each item should remain, shrink, or leave the working set.
scenes.headline: Chapter 5: Memory Lifecycle

scenes.narration: Retain an item when it is verified, likely to affect future decisions, and still has a clear retrieval cue.
scenes.headline: Retain verified items with future decision value

scenes.narration: Distill an item when the event is long but its lesson can be expressed as a fact, rule, checklist, or handoff note. A compact lesson should remain understandable without reopening the entire incident.
scenes.headline: Distill long events into facts, rules, or handoffs

scenes.narration: Forget an item from active memory when it is obsolete, duplicated, low-confidence, or only useful as audit history.
scenes.headline: Retire stale, duplicated, or low-confidence active memory

scenes.narration: Forgetting from the working set is not deleting evidence. Keep the original trace where governance or debugging requires it.
scenes.headline: Retiring working memory does not delete audit evidence

scenes.narration: Review dates matter because a once-correct policy, tool result, or customer preference can become misleading after conditions change.
scenes.headline: Review dates protect against once-correct memories

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, retain durable facts with future decision value.
scenes.headline: Chapter recap. First, retain durable facts.

scenes.narration: Second, distill long experience into a reusable rule or skill.
scenes.headline: Second, distill long experience.

scenes.narration: Third, remove stale or duplicate material from active retrieval without losing the audit trail.
scenes.headline: Third, retire noise without losing the trace.

scenes.narration: Chapter six: Memory Table. Apply the retain–distill–forget decision before your Agent's next long task.
scenes.headline: Chapter 6: Memory Table
scenes.coreLabel: Apply the AI Agent memory tool

scenes.narration: Give every candidate item six fields: the item, its next-task value, its state, its compact form, its retrieval cue, and its review date. This makes a memory decision inspectable instead of hiding it inside a growing prompt.
scenes.headline: Write six fields for every memory candidate
scenes.coreLabel: Item · value · state · form · cue · date

scenes.narration: If a deployment constraint changes permissions, retain the verified constraint with the system and action that need it.
scenes.headline: Retain a verified constraint that changes permissions

scenes.narration: If a troubleshooting session reveals a repeatable fix, distill it into a short skill with a trigger, steps, evidence, and stopping condition. Keep the form short enough to scan during a live task.
scenes.headline: Distill a repeatable repair into a skill

scenes.narration: If five transcripts repeat the same discovery, keep one traceable source and retire the duplicates from active retrieval.
scenes.headline: Keep one traceable source; retire duplicates

scenes.narration: If you cannot name the next decision an item could improve, it probably does not deserve a permanent place in the Agent's working memory.
scenes.headline: No next decision value means no permanent working memory

scenes.narration: Chapter recap. First, write the decision value before saving memory.
scenes.headline: Chapter recap. First, write decision value first.

scenes.narration: Second, choose retain, distill, or forget deliberately.
scenes.headline: Second, choose retain, distill, or forget.

scenes.narration: Third, attach a retrieval cue and review date so memory can stay useful.
scenes.headline: Third, add a cue and review date.

scenes.narration: An AI Agent does not become wiser by carrying every past message into every future task.
scenes.headline: An AI Agent is not wiser because it carries every old message

scenes.narration: Raw history remains useful for audit, but reusable facts and skills are usually better inputs for action.
scenes.headline: Use facts and skills as action-ready inputs

scenes.narration: Route memory from the current decision, then distill the result until the Agent can see what matters without reading the whole past.
scenes.headline: Route from the decision and distill the result

scenes.narration: Use the retain–distill–forget table to make storage, retrieval, and retirement explicit instead of accidental.
scenes.headline: Make retain, distill, and forget explicit choices

scenes.narration: The research result is encouraging, but treat it as evidence for testing your own memory design, not as a universal performance guarantee. Review one retained item after the task to see whether it actually improved the outcome.
scenes.headline: Test this design in your own Agent workflow
